passage: I'm Rajni, and I used to carry my friends' problems home like extra luggage. Vishal, a colleague, began staying back after work to talk about his fights with his brother and his exhaustion, and I listened until 10 pm, then lay awake replaying it. One evening I changed how I did it. I said, "It sounds like you feel he never listens to you. Is that right, or is it something else?" Vishal said it was more that he felt ignored than angry. Then I told him, "I can listen for a while tonight, but I can't be the only one you talk to. Have you thought about the counsellor the company offers?" He looked a little hurt, then said he would look at the details. I went home lighter 🙂, and I still text him next morning.

qa.q: What did Vishal say he felt, after Rajni checked a guess?
qa.a: He said it was more that he felt ignored than angry.

qa.q: How was Rajni feeling when asking "Is that right, or is it something else?"
qa.a: Rajni was unsure whether the guess about Vishal's feelings was right, so Rajni checked; his reply that he felt ignored more than angry showed it was only partly right.

qa.q: What did Rajni change that helped Rajni support Vishal?
qa.a: Rajni checked the guess, set a limit on the evening and suggested the company counsellor.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt when Rajni mentioned the counsellor?
qa.a: He looked a little hurt, perhaps feeling passed along, but he agreed to look at the details, so he may also have found it reasonable.

grounding: A young professional comforts a colleague by checking a guess about his feelings, keeps a limit and refers him to help.

passage: Note from Pranav, team supervisor. On Wednesday I saw Vidya sitting with a colleague who had just received a difficult performance review. She sat at a comfortable distance and let the colleague talk for a while, nodding, before saying, "You sound really discouraged. Am I reading that right?" The colleague said it was more embarrassment than discouragement. Vidya thanked them for correcting her. Later she said, "I'm happy to talk again tomorrow, but I think the company's support service could help with the bigger worry." She gave the colleague the number from the notice board. I noticed Vidya's shoulders were tight afterwards, so I asked how she was. She said she was tired but okay. I have suggested a short break.

qa.q: What did the colleague say the real feeling was?
qa.a: Embarrassment more than discouragement.

qa.q: What might Vidya's tight shoulders suggest about how she felt afterwards?
qa.a: They may suggest she took on some of her colleague's distress and felt tense, though she said she was tired but okay.

qa.q: What could Vidya do to keep supporting others without exhausting herself?
qa.a: She can keep offering to listen while pointing to support services, and take short breaks afterwards, as Pranav suggested. 🙂

qa.q: How might the colleague have felt about Vidya's question "Am I reading that right?"
qa.a: They may have felt understood and free to correct her, since they explained it was embarrassment and not discouragement.

grounding: A young professional listens, checks her reading of a colleague's feelings gently and refers to help, while her own limit shows in her tiredness.

passage:
Wednesday night
Tarun called again at ten, second time this week, about his manager. Forty minutes. I listened, and afterwards I couldn't sleep, replaying his manager's words as if they'd been said to me. I've been carrying his week around like it's mine.
Today I tried something different. At lunch I listened properly for twenty minutes, and when I said, "It sounds like you felt humiliated in that meeting," he shook his head. "Not humiliated. Scared. I think I'm going to lose the job." I'd been guessing wrong all week.
Then I said the thing I'd practised. "I care about this, and I'm glad you tell me. But I'm not enough on my own. The company's counselling line is free and confidential; would you try it? And maybe we keep our chats to lunch, not late at night." He was quiet, then nodded. He booked a session while I was still eating.
Slept well tonight.
Kavitha

qa.q: How long was Tarun's call at ten?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How had Kavitha been feeling after the late calls?
qa.a: Kavitha felt weighed down and sleepless, carrying Tarun's distress as if it were Kavitha's own.

qa.q: How did Kavitha support Tarun while protecting sleep and energy?
qa.a: Kavitha listened fully at lunch, checked the guess about his feelings, suggested the confidential counselling line, and asked to keep chats to lunchtime.

qa.q: What was Tarun actually feeling about his manager?
qa.a: Tarun felt scared about losing his job, not humiliated as Kavitha had guessed.

grounding: Shows a young professional comforting a colleague without absorbing all his distress, checking empathic guesses and referring him to help.

passage:
Sudha: are you up? I can't stop thinking about the layoff
Bidisha: I'm here. tell me
Sudha: I keep replaying the meeting. 12 minutes and my 3 years were done
Sudha: I feel like such a failure
Bidisha: that sounds so painful. is it more shame, or more worry about what's next? just checking I'm reading you right
Sudha: worry mostly. rent, my parents, what I tell people
Bidisha: that makes sense. I'm really glad you told me
Bidisha: I want to be useful, and I'm also fading, I've got a 7am shift. can I call you at lunch tomorrow?
Sudha: yes ok. sorry for keeping you up
Bidisha: no sorry needed 🤍 also, my cousin used the free career counselling at the alumni office after her layoff. want the number?
Sudha: yes please
Bidisha: sending. talk at 1
Sudha: thank you. feel a bit lighter

qa.q: How long did the layoff meeting take?
qa.a: 12 minutes.

qa.q: What was Sudha mainly feeling about the layoff?
qa.a: Sudha felt worried more than ashamed, anxious about rent, family and what to tell people.

qa.q: How did Bidisha support Sudha without overstretching?
qa.a: Bidisha listened, checked the feeling instead of assuming it, set a kind limit with a lunchtime call, and offered a career counselling contact.

qa.q: What would have changed if Bidisha had stayed up talking until 3 am?
qa.a: Bidisha would have been exhausted for the 7 am shift and less able to help later, and Sudha might never have heard about the career counselling.

grounding: Shows a young adult comforting a friend, checking the guessed feeling, keeping a limit and pointing to further help.

passage: By the canal outside the village, Swati talked for almost an hour. Her grandmother had been bedridden since the monsoon, her parents were working in Ludhiana, and Swati was lifting, feeding and washing Dadi alone before and after teaching every day. Vijay listened, handing her the flask of tea. He felt the weight of it settle on his own chest; he wanted to promise he'd fix everything. Instead he checked. "You sound exhausted. Is it more tiredness, or more that you feel alone with it?" Swati wiped her face. "Alone. Tired too, but mostly alone." He nodded. "I can't carry this for you, and I'd do it badly. But the ASHA didi visits bedridden patients, and the women's group at the temple has a rota for helping families. Shall we go to the ASHA didi together tomorrow after school?" Swati let out a breath. "Yes. Together." Walking back, Vijay noticed his own shoulders felt lighter too.

qa.q: Where were Swati's parents working?
qa.a: In Ludhiana.

qa.q: What was Swati mainly feeling, according to her?
qa.a: Swati felt mostly alone with the caring, as well as tired.

qa.q: How did Vijay support Swati without taking on all her distress?
qa.a: He listened, checked his guess about her feelings, admitted he couldn't carry it for her, and offered to go with her to the ASHA didi and the women's group.

qa.q: How might Swati's grandmother benefit from Vijay's suggestion?
qa.a: Dadi could get regular visits from the ASHA didi and help from the women's group, so her care wouldn't depend on one exhausted granddaughter.

grounding: Shows a young adult listening with empathy, checking the guessed feeling, and pointing a friend to local help rather than absorbing it all.

passage:
Every evening that week, Felix stayed after the others left the Melbourne office and talked to Xin: about his manager, his flatmate, his visa papers, how he couldn't sleep. Xin listened. By Thursday she noticed she was lying awake too, going over his problems at 2 am.
On Friday she bought two coffees and sat with him on the front steps. "Can I check something? It sounds like you've been feeling pretty hopeless lately. Is that right, or am I reading too much in?"
Felix was quiet. "Hopeless is close. Tired of everything."
"I'm really glad you tell me things, and I want to keep being here. But I'm not trained for this much, and you deserve someone who is." She showed him the employee support line on her phone. "Would you call them today? I can sit with you while you do."
He called from the steps. She stayed until he had booked a session for Monday.

qa.q: Where did Xin and Felix sit on Friday?
qa.a: They sat on the front steps, with two coffees.

qa.q: Why was Xin lying awake at 2 am?
qa.a: Xin felt worried and weighed down, carrying Felix's problems until they kept her from sleeping.

qa.q: How did Xin balance caring with her own limits?
qa.a: She checked her guess gently, said she wanted to keep being there but wasn't trained for this much, and helped him call the employee support line right then.

qa.q: How might Felix have felt when Xin suggested the support line?
qa.a: Felix may have felt nervous but also cared for, since she stayed with him while he called and booked a session.

grounding: A young professional comforts a colleague without absorbing all his distress, checks her guess about his feelings, and refers him to help the same day.
